channel.title: The Dig — HPC-QC integration and resource management
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the HPC-QC integration and resource management preset. Today’s ranked reading list is led by 2611.30931, a must-read on calibration-insensitive spin-qubit pulses that sustain 99.97% fidelity and stable rotation angles over ten days in Si/SiGe, directly targeting drift and recalibration. The remaining skims span adjacent practical concerns: 2611.32388 offers shallow-circuit thermal-state preparation ideas transferable mainly through depth reduction; 2611.30508 and 2611.32560 provide low-resource QAOA constructions and application heuristics relevant to small noisy spin-qubit benchmarks; 2611.29983 presents a calibration-aware compilation and backend stack but lacks spin-qubit and HPC evidence; and 2611.31514 frames DOE-scale HPC-quantum integration strategy without concrete spin-qubit control or middleware methods. No pay dirt today — 2 to skim.

item.title: Cqlib: A High-Performance Software Stack for Quantum Computing
item.description:
Skim new method — Cqlib 2.0 provides an end-to-end quantum computing software stack in native Rust with Python and C interfaces, verifying structural and semantic correctness across Benchpress parameterized compilation tasks while generating Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS) instructions for hardware execution.

Grade 0.658 · 4.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Integration of Quantum Accelerators with High Performance Computing—A Review of…”

Figure

The structural workflow showing program transformations from high-level circuit construction through Rust-based compilation down to QCIS hardware instructions and backend execution.

Asks

How can quantum programming workflows combine unified circuit semantics, multilingual high performance, and direct compilation to hardware-level control instruction sets like QCIS?

Before

Cqlib was previously a cloud-specific software interface restricted to supporting Tianyan Quantum Cloud experiments.

But

Evaluated only on the specific compilation and circuit-construction task scopes covered in Benchpress and reported test sets.

Tools

Rust core engine · Python and C FFI interfaces · Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS) · OpenQASM parser and generator · Benchpress benchmark suite

Abstract

This paper presents Cqlib, a high-performance software stack for quantum computing built around a unified quantum circuit model. Its native Rust core provides efficient implementations of circuit processing, quantum-state and operator computation, compilation, and optimization, while Python and C interfaces support algorithm development and system integration. Cqlib covers quantum program construction, simulation, analysis, compilation, device adaptation, and result processing under consistent program semantics. Through OpenQASM and the Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS), Cqlib supports program representation and hardware-oriented execution. Cqlib further provides backend interfaces for device execution, with Cqlib-Tianyan serving as one implementation for QCIS-compatible quantum hardware. Evaluations using parameterized compilation tasks from Benchpress and related tests show that Cqlib achieves good functional coverage, compilation correctness, and execution efficiency within the evaluated task scope. We develop Cqlib-Algorithm as a modular library of reusable operators and composable components for widely used quantum algorithms, including quantum search, phase estimation, and variational algorithms, with additional support for error mitigation. To complement these building blocks with domain-specific workflows, we further develop Cqlib-VQE, Cqlib-QAOA, and Cqlib-QML for application-level studies in quantum chemistry, combinatorial optimization, and quantum machine learning, respectively. Cqlib also integrates source-grounded Skills and MCP-based tools to support agent-assisted program generation, backend execution, and result-guided workflow refinement. Overall, Cqlib provides a unified and extensible software foundation that connects quantum algorithm development, simulation, compilation, and execution on QCIS-compatible quantum hardware.

item.title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing
item.description:
Skim review — Proposes DOE deployment strategy targeting initial FTQCs by 2028 with ≥100 logical qubits performing 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations, scaling to production systems of 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits performing 109 to 1010 hard logical operations in the 2030s.

Grade 0.652 · 4.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Computers for High-Performance Computing” · Ryan Bennink, Robin Blume-Kohout, Salman Habib, Andrew Landahl, Hai Ah Nam, Laura Schulz, Mallikarjun Shankar, Nicholas Wright

Asks

What roadmap, milestones, and infrastructure does the US Department of Energy need to integrate fault-tolerant quantum supercomputers into national scientific computing?

But

Contingent on commercial hardware roadmap progress and realization of low-overhead quantum error correction.

Tools

fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) · supercomputing integration roadmap · hardware-software co-design

Abstract

Quantum computing stands at the threshold of a transformative decade, where the field will evolve from small-scale demonstrations toward practical scientific computing at scale. This Blueprint identifies fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) as a viable, scalable, and broadly applicable path to achieving "quantum scientific utility." It outlines a strategy to prepare the US Department of Energy (DOE) for FTQCs and their integration into the US national scientific computing infrastructure. Its purpose is to identify the steps, milestones, and research directions necessary for DOE to enable initial deployment of FTQCs in 2028 as a scientific tool for the nation and mature this capability into the 2030s. Given recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected logical qubits and the advancement of commercial hardware roadmaps, DOE should begin preparations for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment for DOE science missions. This Blueprint proposes that DOE focus on (1) deploying first-generation scientifically relevant quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits and performing at least 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations in scientifically relevant calculations; (2) developing essential FTQC programming competencies, system software, and facility readiness; and (3) investing in cutting-edge focused R&D that fosters breakthroughs in scientific applications, algorithms, and logical architectures needed to accelerate the advent of scientific utility. This effort will position DOE to transition to larger systems: production-scale quantum computers that comprise 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, perform 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations, and execute scientifically useful computations at scale. The Blueprint calls for transformative R&D and collective action to accelerate the advent of scientific quantum utility and bring it within reach by 2028.
